content: Within Physlib, we already have electromagnetism for an isotropic and homogeneous medium. I was wondering if we could make a push in PhyslibAlpha to generalize some of these results so that maybe we can define Snell's law and start relating it to optics. Then we can have a full connection of results from QED on one side to optics on the other side.
If people are interested in this, how do you think we should organize such an endeavor? Maybe we could form a Tau Ceti sort of approach.

I had thought about this, and I want to make sure we're on the same page. What do you have in mind for this on the optics side?

for me there are two difficulties in defining refraction:

  1. how to define the material
  2. how to define the boundary (or how does Maxwell apply in relation to it)


(^Claude used in image preparation)

My understanding is something like this. My dream would be to go for the top-left which is most general, then we derive the macroscopic description (left to right in the diagram) and existence of a reflected and refracted wave via Ewald-Oseen extinction theorem (which would be a significant project). Going from top to bottom is the standard Gaussian pillbox argument, which needs an interface API, or equivalently a distributional statement about the derivative of a half-space indicator, which doesn't (ideally also the Divergence/Stokes API to connect the two). Separately from the square, defining refraction also needs a solution class (fixed frequency, a given incident plane wave, outgoing condition), and Snell is actually a property of that class, not of the medium.

this part I think needs careful design and I would push back on an AI led effort.
having said that, I believe what you want is something simpler: let me try sketching it out

I'm not familiar with QED ideas so correct me if I'm wrong, we would just want to tie things to IsExtrema, and one way to do that is as following:

  1. A medium is a refractive-index distribution over all of space. For refraction it's piecewise constant across a plane.
  2. The medium enters only as bound charge and current, fed into the vacuum equations we already have. So the dynamical statement is still IsExtrema, with the current set to free plus bound.
  3. Because the equations hold across the plane and not just on each side, the jump conditions are consequences: the derivative of a discontinuous polarisation has a surface term, and that term is the bound surface charge. The only new analytic ingredient is a lemma about the derivative of a half-space indicator in the existing distribution framework. This is the pillbox argument in distributional form.
  4. Refraction itself is a solution class, separate from the medium: fixed frequency, a given incident plane wave, and an outgoing condition on everything else. Snell is a property of that class, with the tangential wavevector conserved because the jump conditions must hold at every point of the plane, and Fresnel is the linear system which the jump conditions impose on the amplitudes.

(after some back and forth with claude, may not be fully polished)

This I think is doable, which hopefully is close to what you have in mind.

Yes, this is close to what I had in mind. I was unsure if the distributional framework was itself general enough to do what we wanted, but if it is, then maybe we should push in that direction (but not necessarily fully AI-led). Maybe human-guided and with AI assistance.

I think we don't even have things like magnetization defined in Physlib yet, and maybe this is something that is within easy reach.
